units: the clay delivered to the workshop loses its moisture far too quickly
paste that is too dry breaks and the walls give way before the kiln
the craftsman wraps every block in a soaked cloth
the blocks are kept away from heat and from drafts
this treatment makes the paste supple again and easy to throw
the dust that settles on damp pieces spoils the glaze
a sheet of cloth has been stretched above the shelves
the floor is wetted before every throwing session
the vessels leave the kiln with a smooth and soft look
the potter credits the result to the care given to what surrounds the work
text: Clay reaches the pottery in dark blocks, and it gives up its moisture far too fast for the work that has to follow. Try to raise a pot from paste that dry and it crumbles: the walls split, they sag, and the piece is lost long before the kiln ever sees it. The potter's answer is a patient one. He wraps every block in a soaked cloth and sets it aside, out of the heat, clear of any draft that crosses the room. The clay softens again, yields under the palm, and climbs easily on the wheel. One trouble stayed. Dust drifts down onto the damp pieces and dulls the glaze, so he stretched a fine sheet above the shelves and wets the floor before he sits down to throw. The bowls now leave the kiln with a smooth, quiet skin. Ask him why that works and he will not talk about his hands. He talks about what surrounds them.

units: the author sets two ways of joining the pieces of a timber frame against each other
the traditional joint spreads the forces through the thickness of the wood
this joint grows tighter as it ages
fixing with bolts piles up stress around the holes
repeated shaking weakens the metal piece
the argument from speed ignores what later repairs cost
strength is measured by the ability to move without breaking
seasoned practitioners set a piece according to the way the tree grew
this judgment cannot be handed over to a machine
the author judges a technique on how long it stays in use
text: Set a pegged timber frame beside a bolted one and a badly framed argument comes into view. Cut joinery hands the load off into the body of the wood, and the years only draw it tighter. Bolts do the reverse. Stress gathers at the drilled holes, and shaking, season after season, leaves the steel brittle. People praise the speed of the bolted method and quietly forget what the patching will cost. A sound frame is not the one that holds best through its first winter. It is the one that can move and still not break. Carpenters trained the old way read the grain, dodge the knots, and lay each piece as the tree grew. No machine makes that call. To defend them is not to pine for anything; it is to say that a method is judged by how long it stays in use, not by how fast it goes up.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described binds books and is held by her colleagues to be experienced
she learned the trade beside a master who did not speak
that master corrected her way of working through gesture
her equipment includes bone tools, a sewing frame and presses of old wood
she works with leathers, undyed cloth and papers decorated in a bath
she takes on two students every season
she picks them for their stamina rather than for their skill
she holds failure to be more instructive than success
she keeps her own old mistakes at home
her bindings sit in research collections and carry no name
text: The binder in question has worked enough winters at the trade that her peers treat her as a thoroughly seasoned hand. Her life sorts into a few plain headings. Training first: she learned beside a master who never spoke a word to her and who set her hands right by moving them himself. Tools next, bone folders, a sewing frame, wooden presses whose knotted uprights groan at every turn of the screw. Materials after that, soft skins, undyed cloth, marbled papers floated off a bath. Teaching last. Each season she takes on two apprentices, and she picks them for stamina rather than for a deft touch. A binding that failed, she says, teaches more than one that came out right, and she keeps her own early wrecks in a drawer at home. Her books sit in study libraries, none of them signed.

units: the visit follows the order the designers intended
the opening room shows unsharpened blades straight out of the forge
the critic finds this first part clear and bare
the second section brings together tools that have been used
one cutting tool carries a nick left by a flaw in the wood
another tool shows an edge worn down by repeated use
the explanatory texts stay easy to follow without losing precision
the third room mixes the trades together and loses the visitor
the end of the visit shows silent images of hands at work
the verdict is favourable despite a weakening at the middle of the show
text: The show on cutting tools is walked through in the order its makers laid out, and that order is what carries it. The opening room holds unground blades, straight from the forge, still black with scale; the point being made is clear and the staging is bare. Then come the tools that have worked for a living, and the interest rises. A chisel chipped where a hard knot ran through the board. A plane whose dulled iron records thousands of passes. The labels stay plain without ever going vague. The third room is where the thing slips. Cases pile up, trades run together, and the thread you were handed comes loose in your fingers. The closing stretch wins some of that back with footage of hands at work, silent, no music laid over it. You leave persuaded by the whole, even with that dip through the middle.

units: the writer answers a question about whether his workshop is running well
the seat he built would not stand straight
the cause is a joint made on wood that was not dry enough
the wood shrank as it dried and the joint went slack
the writer took the whole thing apart
a craftsman nearby had warned him
he let the wood dry for a full season before starting again
the joints now hold and the finish comes easily
he blames his haste rather than any lack of skill
he asks to borrow a hollowing tool because his own is finished
text: You asked whether the workshop is finally running the way it should, so here it is straight. The stool I put together this winter never sat flat on the floor. I had driven the tenons home into wood that was still green. It shrank as it dried, the joint went slack, and the seat ended up rocking under anyone who sat on it. So I pulled the whole thing apart, every piece of it. The old joiner in the shed next door had warned me, and this time I listened. The boards sat breathing a whole season before I began again. Now the joints hold, and the surface that fought me under the first sanding takes a polish with almost no work. What went wrong was my hurry, not my hands. If you come by, bring your curved gouge. Mine is finished and I dare not hollow a seat without one. Write soon, and tell me whether your kiln is drawing.

units: a guild of weaving craftsmen watches its plantations weaken
the shoots they cut have grown shorter and snap while being worked
worn-out soil is held to blame
cutting too often wears the roots of the plant down
the plots are now worked at wider intervals
organic matter is worked into the soil
older and suppler varieties have been put back into the ground
the crop fell by a third the first season and then climbed again
the spokesman for the group grants that the objects sold cost more
the collective teaches beginners a way of cutting that was nearly given up
text: What becomes of a trade when the raw material it lives on begins to thin out? Put to a guild of basket weavers whose willow beds are failing, the question drew an answer in three parts. The finding first: the rods they cut come up shorter than they used to and snap in the weave. The diagnosis next. Tired soil, and roots cut back far too often, leave the plants with nothing left to push out. Then the fix, two seasons old already, longer rotations between the plots, compost worked into the ground, older and suppler varieties planted again. Their spokesman says the crop dropped by a third that first season before it climbed back. Asked about the price of a basket, he grants that it has gone up and stands by it. The guild now teaches newcomers to cut, a skill almost no workshop was still handing down.

units: a stone craftsman teaches his pupil that every block calls for its own hand
the first stone has a rough texture and hard grains
this stone rings clearly when it is struck
the second stone is softer and takes a smooth finish
the pupil wants to know which of the two is better
the master refuses to compare the materials against each other
he says that only the intended use settles it
the rough stone suits a step because it keeps a foot from slipping
the smooth stone suits a ledge because water runs off it
the master says the pupil will stop asking this one evening
text: The stonecutter kept telling his apprentice that no two blocks ever ask for the same hand. The first one, he said, is coarse, packed with hard grains that catch the point and ring bright under the mallet. The other is softer, takes the rasp kindly, and comes up satin, almost disconcertingly smooth against the palm. The apprentice wanted to know which of the two was the better stone. The question means nothing at all, the cutter answered: you do not weigh one stone against another, you weigh what is being asked of each. A stair tread wants the rough block, the one a boot cannot slide on. A window ledge wants the other, which water washes over and then leaves. Then he wiped the white dust off his forearms and added that the apprentice would know how to choose alone, the evening he stopped asking.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the way metal casting workshops changed is set out theme by theme
burnt wood was given up for a denser fuel
this change raised the heat reached in the vats
the air devices were worked by human strength at first
they were later driven by the force of water
this shift made the rise in heat steady
packed sand took the place of clay for shaping the impressions
this material stands up better to shifts of heat and pulls away without breaking
a measured addition of tin gave a metal that took knocks better
a post for watching the furnace appeared and cut into the founder's authority
text: The history of the casting workshops is best taken one strand at a time. Fuel to begin with: charred wood gave way to denser coals, and the vats ran a good deal hotter for it. Bellows come next. Arms worked them at first, then water turned the wheels that drove them, and the heat rose steadily instead of by fits and starts. Moulds after that, where rammed sand took the place of raw clay, since it stands up far better to sudden shifts of heat and lifts away without cracking. Alloys last of all, where a measured share of tin yielded a metal that rang under a blow without splitting. Each of these developments rearranged the work itself. The founder surrendered part of his authority to the hand watching the furnace, a responsibility that had existed in none of these workshops before.

units: the worker gathers a quantity of molten glass on the end of his rod
this mass is almost running at the moment it is taken up
it is rolled on a metal surface to bring it true and stiffen its skin
blowing air in opens a cavity inside the mass
short reheats alternate with the shaping stages
glass that has gone cold splits at the slightest knock
the opening at the top is widened with a tool that pinches
the piece is then passed to a helper
a last stay in an oven brings the heat down slowly through the night
without this gradual cooling the object would break of its own accord
text: The blower starts by dipping his pipe into the melt and lifting out a thick orange lump that barely holds its own weight as it comes. He rolls it along a steel plate to bring it true and to stiffen the skin of it. Then the first breath: a bubble opens in the heart of the mass and swells out as the air pushes. From there he trades short reheats for shaping, over and over, because glass that has gone cold turns brittle and splits at the slightest knock. Once the belly is right, he spreads the neck open with a pair of jacks, breaks the piece free, and passes it across to a helper. The last stage happens in an annealing oven, where the heat steps down all night long. Without that carefully managed descent, the strain locked inside would in time crack the vessel apart where it stands on the shelf.

units: a damaged drain pipe let water through above a gilding workshop
the store room was reached by the leak
the thin metal leaves kept there are extremely light
the paper sheets between them buckled under the water
the leaves welded to one another and could no longer be used
the want of supplies halted the repair of an old frame
the woman who had ordered the work saw her date pushed back
the accident had consequences for three other trades
the store was moved lower down and shut into a closed cabinet
a notebook now records the state of the lots at every withdrawal
text: A cracked gutter running over the gilding workshop was enough to wreck a whole season of work. Water crept its way into the store room, where beaten gold leaf lay waiting, so thin that a single breath will carry it off. The tissue sheets between them buckled in the wet, the leaves welded into one another, and the whole lot was finished. With nothing left to work from, the gilder had to stop midway through an old frame, which pushed back the woman who had ordered it, and she had a date of her own to keep. The delay ran outward and caught a joiner, a varnisher and a carrier as well. Out of it came a rule she holds to now: the store came down to floor level, into a shut cabinet, and a notebook records the state of every lot each time it is opened. The roof still leaks. The gold stays dry.
